title: Reasoning well: arguments, evidence and fallacies
purpose: Spot arguments in everyday talk, pick out premises and conclusions, tell valid from invalid reasoning with simple patterns, judge evidence and sources, reason carefully about samples, causes and chances, recognize common fallacies and biases, and disagree respectfully.
primary_reading: Wireless Philosophy (Wi-Phi) on Khan Academy: critical thinking videos

weeks.1: What is an argument? Premises and conclusions
weeks.2: Finding arguments in ads, news and conversation
weeks.3: Deductive validity: if the premises are true, must the conclusion be?
weeks.4: Valid patterns: modus ponens, modus tollens and the syllogism
weeks.6: Evidence, sources and how much to trust a claim
weeks.8: Chance and probability in everyday reasoning
weeks.9: Fallacies of relevance: attacking the person, the straw man and appeals to popularity
weeks.10: Fallacies of ambiguity and presumption: equivocation, false dilemma and begging the question
weeks.12: Disagreeing well: charity, the strongest version of a view and changing your mind

blocks.deliverable: Mark the premises and conclusion in ten short passages.
Sort twelve arguments into valid and invalid.
Rate five sources for a claim and explain each rating.
Week 7 midterm; explain why a correlation does not prove a cause.
Name the fallacy in ten short arguments.
Rewrite a flawed argument as the strongest version you can.
Submit the project; take an unseen 45 minute final in week 14.

project: Argument portfolio: collect five real arguments from ads, news articles or conversations, map each into premises and a conclusion, judge whether it is valid or strong and whether its premises are true, name any fallacies, and rewrite the weakest one as the best argument for its conclusion that you can make.
completion: finish the project, take the week 7 midterm and week 14 cumulative final, then complete a new cumulative assessment after 1 to 2 weeks. Explain one major idea aloud without notes.
